extracted.intended_audience: economists, policy analysts, and researchers studying patents, appropriability, and industry innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and measurement framework for how effective patents and alternative mechanisms are at appropriating returns from new processes and products across industries, based on survey questions, principal components, and cluster analyses. Includes metrics on limitations of patents, channels of information spillover, imitation cost/time, and motives for patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents to prevent duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item asking how effective patents are in preventing competitors from duplicating new processes and products (separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on a 1-to-7 scale (1 = not at all effective; 7 = very effective). Results reported by industry and aggregated; product patents tended to be rated more effective than process patents in most industries, with chemical industries highest. Correlates with effectiveness at securing royalty income; used as one of six mechanisms of appropriation in principal components and cluster analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents to secure royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item asking how effective patents are in securing royalty income from new processes and products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on the same 1-to-7 effectiveness scale. Often correlated with 'patents to prevent duplication.' Industry means reported; used as a distinct appropriability dimension in factor/principal components analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy as a means of appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Secrecy (keeping a technology confidential) as an alternative mechanism for appropriating returns from innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyed for effectiveness separately for processes and products (1–7 scale). Secrecy clusters with lead time and learning-curve advantages for processes; its effectiveness is positively correlated with the extent to which patent disclosures limit patent usefulness. Used in PCA and cluster analyses as a nonpatent appropriation mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead time as a means of appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using first-mover or lead-time advantages to appropriate returns from new processes or products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on the 1–7 scale; often groups with learning-curve and secrecy advantages as a nonpatent dimension. Cluster analyses identify industries where lead time is a primary appropriation mechanism. Guidance notes that lead time effectiveness differs by industry and by whether the innovation is a product or process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moving down the learning curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Capturing returns by achieving cost reductions and efficiency through learning-curve progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 1–7 for both processes and products. Typically groups with lead time in factor analyses. Cluster results show some industries rely primarily on learning-curve advantages rather than patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales and service efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using superior sales and after-sales service to appropriate returns from new products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured separately for products (and less applicable to processes) on the 1–7 scale. For products, sales/service effectiveness is strongly linked to lead time and learning advantages. Often the top-rated nonpatent mechanism for product appropriability in many industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal components: patent vs nonpatent dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimensional reduction identifying two main appropriability dimensions: one associated with patents and the other with nonpatent mechanisms (secrecy, lead time, learning curves, sales/service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal components analysis on the six process questions and six product questions shows the first component places near-zero weight on patents and heavy weight on other mechanisms (nonpatent); the second component places heavy weight on patent-related methods. The two components explain only ~50–60% of variance, so interpretation is clear but incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster analysis of mechanisms of appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of industries into clusters according to mean responses on the six appropriation mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best solution divided industries into three clusters: (1) low scores for all mechanisms with sales/service relatively highest; (2) industries rating lead time and learning curves highly but not patents; (3) industries where product and process patents are effective. Caution: within-cluster variance is almost twice between-cluster variance, so clusters are suggestive rather than definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitors legally 'invent around' patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: the ability of competitors to invent around both process and product patents reduces patent effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on a 1–7 scale in Table 5; 'invent around' was rated higher than five by 60% of responding industries, indicating it is a major constraint. This limitation is strongly implicated in reducing the practical appropriability of patents across many sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents unlikely to be valid if challenged (validity/invalidation risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: patents may be unlikely to withstand legal challenges, reducing their effectiveness as protective instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey respondents rated this limitation for processes and products; several industries (e.g., food processing, fabricated metals) scored this >5 meaningfully. The paper notes interindustry clusters where invalidity is a serious perceived problem and links to potential causes (mature industries, difficulty proving novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Firms do not enforce patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: patent holders may choose not to enforce patents, lowering their deterrent and appropriation value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a distinct limitation in Table 5 (rated 1–7). Non-enforcement interacts with other limitations and affects perceived patent effectiveness; industry means and distribution reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology moving so fast that patents are irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: rapid technological change can make patent protection irrelevant by the time protection is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on the 1–7 scale; considered generally more severe for processes than products. Appears in Table 5 as a notable but not universally dominant constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent documents disclose too much information (disclosure effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: disclosures required in patent documents can facilitate inventing-around and reduce patent effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyed for both processes and products; disclosure was a substantial limitation for relatively few industries (4 for products, 16 for processes at high ratings). The paper links disclosure severity to higher effectiveness of secrecy and notes the disclosure effect is stronger for products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing required by court decisions (compulsory licensing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: compulsory licensing imposed by legal decisions can reduce patent effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated in Table 5; overall judged rarely significant (only a few industries rated this >5). The paper contrasts perceived importance with prior literature and policy discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firms participate in cross-licensing agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation/feature: widespread cross-licensing can reduce exclusive appropriation value of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among limitations in Table 5. The practice may moderate the exclusivity function of patents and was measured across industries; the paper mentions cross-licensing’s strategic role (e.g., semiconductors) earlier in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Licensing technology
rubrics_metrics.description: One channel by which rivals learn about an innovator's technology — licensing agreements or explicit transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated for effectiveness in learning about processes and products (1–7). Licensing correlates with patent disclosures and, when patents are effective, is a primary channel for learning. Used in cluster analyses of spillover channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Patent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents as an information channel by which rivals can learn about new technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 1–7 for processes and products. Correlated with licensing effectiveness; may serve as an 'announcement' or 'complementary information' effect. Strength of correlation differs by product vs process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Publications or technical meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpersonal/public channels (papers, conferences) through which firms learn about competitors' R&D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on 1–7 scale; strongly intercorrelated with other interpersonal channels (conversations, hiring). Cluster analysis identifies industries where interpersonal channels dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Conversations with employees of innovating firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal interpersonal exchanges as a learning mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyed and reported with standard errors. Correlates strongly with publications/meetings and hiring; part of an interpersonal cluster of spillover channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Hiring R&D employees from innovating firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning-by-hiring as a channel for acquiring competitor know-how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 1–7 and appears in the interpersonal cluster. The paper notes hiring correlates with other interpersonal learning mechanisms and is an important source of spillovers in some industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Reverse engineering of product
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning by disassembling and analyzing competitors' products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markedly more effective for products than processes. Reverse engineering correlates negatively with patent effectiveness and is an important channel in industries where patents are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of learning: Independent R&D
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning through a firm's own R&D effort that reveals or approximates competitors' innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On average the most effective reported means of learning about rival technology. Rated highly across industries and often groups with licensing in cluster analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of duplicating an innovation (percentage of innovator's R&D cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents estimated duplication cost as a percentage of the innovator's R&D cost for categories of innovations (major vs typical; patented vs unpatented; product vs process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as frequency distributions of industry medians. Findings: duplicating major innovations costs more and takes longer than typical ones; patents tend to raise imitation costs (quantified examples: patents raise imitation costs by ~40 percentage points for major and typical new drugs, ~30 for major chemical products, ~7–15 for electronics). Coding on interval scales used for statistical tests; interindustry differences sometimes insignificant due to intraindustry variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time required to duplicate an innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents estimated time-to-duplicate using intervals (e.g., <6 months, 6 months–1 year, 1–3 years, 3–5 years, >5 years, not possible) for the same innovation categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time responses show significant interindustry variation (significant at 0.01 in most comparisons). Patents generally increase the time required to duplicate innovations, and the association between reported patent effectiveness and time-to-duplicate is especially strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patents on imitation cost/time (patent increases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured increase in duplication costs and time associated with presence of patents, correlated with reported patent effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each innovation category authors computed mean increases attributable to patents and correlated these with effectiveness ratings; positive correlations found for all categories, stronger for products than processes. Some anomalies observed where patents coincided with lower duplication costs (often where disclosures were an issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of new processes or products
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which new processes or products are patentable — viewed as a precondition affecting patent effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of patentability was rated an important limitation (higher for processes than products). Reported industry responses indicate this is a significant constraint in many sectors and informs policy discussions about adjusting legal patentability standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-appropriation motives for patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives for filing patents that are not directly about appropriating R&D returns (e.g., measuring R&D employee performance; gaining access to foreign markets requiring licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed qualitatively based on respondents' comments and pretests: patents may be used to evaluate inventors/team production, to enable licensing requirements of host countries, or strategically to build portfolios for cross-licensing. These reasons can explain patenting behavior even where patents are perceived as weak appropriation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey measurement, statistical reporting, and interpretation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a 1–7 Likert scale, reporting of means and standard errors, aggregation to industry means and medians, significance testing for interindustry differences, and presentation of principal components/cluster solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors provide standard errors in parentheses, report ranges of industry means, note significance levels (.10, .05, .01) for interindustry differences, and caution about variance explained by PCA and clustering fit. Tables (e.g., Tables 2–9) summarize these measurements and statistical qualifications; correlations and robustness checks (individual respondent vs industry mean units) are discussed.
